Vishnushaman.description: The narrator who tells the story to the princes.

Swift.description: A wise and cautious crow who lives in the banyan tree and is a friend to the other animal characters.

Gay-Neck.description: A dove-king who leads a flock of doves and is caught in the hunter's snare.

Ravan.description: A figure from the Indian epic Ramayana, known for abducting Sita.

Rama.description: A hero of the Ramayana, husband of Sita, and slayer of Ravan.

Yudhishthir.description: A principal character from the Mahabharata, known for his righteousness but also for his weakness for gambling.

Book II.description: The second book of the Panchatantra, titled 'The Winning of Friends,' focusing on friendship and cooperation.

Maidens’ Delight.description: A city in the southern country where part of the story takes place.

banyan tree.description: A large, sacred fig tree native to India, known for its aerial roots and cultural significance.

Bharunda.description: A mythical bird with two necks and a single belly, symbolizing the dangers of disunity; its story illustrates the importance of unity.

snare.description: A trap for catching birds or animals, typically made of a noose of wire or cord.

club.description: A heavy stick used as a weapon.

noose.description: A loop with a running knot, tightening as the rope or wire is pulled, used for trapping.

incarnation.description: The embodiment of a deity or spirit in earthly form, often used in Indian religious context.

unrighteousness.description: Lack of moral virtue or justice; wickedness.

mesh.description: The netting or network of a snare or trap.

dissuasion.description: The act of advising against something.

Gold.description: A mouse skilled in social ethics, who helps free the doves and becomes friends with Swift.

Slow.description: A turtle living by a lake in the jungle, an old friend of Swift the crow.

Indra.description: King of the gods in Hindu mythology, referenced in proverbs about oaths and enmity.

Diti.description: A figure in Hindu mythology, mother of demons, referenced in a proverb about Indra.

Panini.description: A legendary Sanskrit grammarian, referenced as an example of a scholar killed by a beast.

Jaimini.description: A sage and philosopher in Indian tradition, referenced as a victim of a mad elephant.

Pingal.description: An ancient Indian scholar of prosody, referenced as being killed by a crocodile.

dhak-blossom.description: A bright red flower (Butea monosperma) native to India, used as a simile for the color of meat.

Arcturus.description: A bright star, referenced in a proverb about the ocean waiting for its contribution.

retinue.description: A group of attendants or followers accompanying an important person.

fortress-den.description: A fortified or well-protected animal burrow or home.

qui vive.description: An archaic phrase meaning 'on the alert' or 'watchful.'

servants.description: Those who serve a master; in this context, animal followers.

toothache.description: A sudden pain in a tooth, here used humorously as a possible interruption.

triple world.description: A concept from Indian cosmology referring to the three realms: heaven, earth, and the underworld.

bosom friend.description: A very close and dear friend.

twing.description: Likely a variant or archaic spelling of 'twig,' a small branch.

Full-Flight.description: A named type of bird flight, part of a list of eight flight types.

Crop-Ear.description: A hermit living near a shrine to Shiva who struggles to protect his food hoard from a clever mouse, whom he views as a villain.

Wide-Bottom.description: A holy man and guest of Crop-Ear, known for his pious tales and forthright manner.

Mother Shandilee.description: A character representing practical wisdom in a proverb about sesame grain, whose identity is confirmed by Kamandaki, the son of a householder.

Shiva.description: A major Hindu deity, worshipped as the destroyer and transformer within the Trimurti.

alms-bowl.description: A bowl used by hermits or monks to collect food given as charity.

dainties.description: Delicate or choice foods, often sweet or specially prepared.

treacle.description: A thick, sweet syrup made during the refining of sugar; similar to molasses.

ordinance.description: A prescribed religious or moral rule or practice.

contrition.description: Sincere remorse or penitence for wrongdoing.

chaplain.description: A clergy member attached to a private chapel, institution, or group.

abbot.description: The head of a monastery or community of monks.

recompense.description: Compensation or reward given for loss or effort.

bamboo.description: A fast-growing woody grass, often used in India for tools and construction.

hulled.description: With the outer covering or husk removed, especially referring to grains.

unhulled.description: With the outer covering or husk still present, especially referring to grains.

mouse-hole.description: The hole or burrow where a mouse lives, often used metaphorically for a hiding place.

Brahman.description: A pious man and his skeptical wife who discuss the merits of charitable giving and the struggles of their poverty.

Scriptures.description: Sacred Hindu texts that provide moral and religious guidance.

betimes.description: An archaic English word meaning early or at an early hour.

mite.description: A small amount, often used to refer to a tiny contribution or offering.

solstice.description: The time when the sun is at its greatest distance from the celestial equator, marking the change of seasons.

pious.description: Devoutly religious or showing reverence for religious duties.

hillman.description: A hunter who attempts to kill a boar and is killed in turn; his body, along with the boar's, is later found by a starving jackal and his wife who die due to their own greed.

boar.description: A wild animal that is hunted by the hillman and kills him before dying from an arrow wound.

cat.description: A predatory animal that attacks the pack of mice.

mice.description: Followers of the narrator, who suffer losses from the cat and later abandon their leader.

Sooty Mountain.description: A mountain referenced to describe the appearance of the boar.

Himalaya.description: A famous mountain range in India, mentioned in a proverb about danger.

shaft.description: An archaic term for an arrow.

bow-string.description: The string of a bow, used to shoot arrows.

sinew.description: A tendon, often used for binding or as a string in traditional bows.

elixir.description: A magical or medicinal potion, often believed to grant health or immortality.

dowrl.description: An archaic or possibly misprinted word, likely meant to be 'dowrl' or 'dowry', referring to a precious drink or item.

topknot.description: A tuft of hair or ornament worn on the top of the head.

sesame.description: An oilseed crop, often used in Indian cuisine and rituals.

alms.description: Charitable donations, usually of food or money, given to the poor or holy men.

pickaxe.description: A tool with a heavy metal head used for digging.

prodigious.description: Remarkably or impressively great in extent, size, or degree.

uncouth.description: Strange or clumsy in appearance or manner; uncivilized.

tufted.description: Having or adorned with a tuft or tufts.

dole.description: A charitable gift of food, money, or clothing.

tramp.description: A person who travels from place to place on foot, often in search of work or as a vagrant.

moneybag.description: A bag for holding money; here, used metaphorically for wealth.

crow-barley.description: A type of wild barley, often considered of little value.

buffets.description: Blows or strikes, especially with the hand.

cars of heaven.description: Mythological reference to divine chariots or vehicles.

beggar.description: A person who lives by asking for charity.

monk.description: A member of a religious community, often living in poverty and chastity.

Mister Duly.description: The son of a merchant named Ocean, he is known for his repetitive phrase 'What’s duly his, a man receives' and mistakenly marries Naughty.

Moonlight.description: A princess in the story, young and beautiful, who falls in love at first sight with a prince.

Fine-Fame.description: A bridegroom from another district who arrives for his wedding but flees when an elephant runs amuck.

Naughty.description: The policeman’s daughter, a young and beautiful girl who mistakenly marries Mister Duly in the darkness.

rupees.description: The currency of India, used here to indicate the price paid for the book.

Brahman-slayer.description: A Sanskrit cultural reference to someone who commits the grave sin of killing a Brahmin, considered one of the worst sins.

Vishnu.description: A major Hindu deity, referenced here as the universal lord.

Mount Meru.description: A sacred mountain in Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist cosmology, considered the center of all physical, metaphysical, and spiritual universes.

thanatophidian.description: A scientific term referring to venomous snakes, derived from Greek but used in Indian context here.

lord of seven continents.description: A reference to the ancient Indian cosmological concept of a ruler who controls all the world's continents.

wigging.description: An archaic English term meaning a scolding or reprimand.

stucco.description: A fine plaster used for coating wall surfaces or molding into architectural decorations.

sang-froid.description: A French-origin term meaning composure or coolness, sometimes excessive, as shown in danger or under trying circumstances.

tomtoms.description: Indian drums used in processions and celebrations.

amuck.description: A term of Malay origin meaning to behave uncontrollably and disruptively.

ablossom.description: An archaic or poetic term meaning in full bloom or blossoming.

date.description: In this context, an appointment or meeting, especially of a romantic nature.

finery.description: Expensive or ostentatious clothes or decoration, especially for a special occasion.

crown prince.description: The male heir apparent to the throne.

leagues.description: An old unit of distance, roughly three miles.

draughts.description: An archaic term for drinks or doses of liquid.

continent.description: In this context, refers to the large landmasses of the world, but also used in Indian cosmology.

charity.description: The voluntary giving of help, typically in the form of money, to those in need.

Soft.description: A weaver who struggles to earn more than food and clothes, despite his skill and efforts.

Doer.description: A supernatural figure representing the agent of actions or fate, who debates with Deed about Soft's fortune.

Deed.description: A supernatural figure representing the consequences of actions, who interacts with Doer regarding Soft's fate.

Growing City.description: A city to which Soft moves in hopes of earning more money.

cowrie.description: A type of shell historically used as currency in India and other parts of Asia.

fiendish.description: Having the qualities of a fiend; extremely wicked or cruel.

spear-grass.description: A type of tough grass, often used for making ropes in India.

capital.description: Wealth in the form of money or assets.

base-born.description: Of low or humble birth; not noble.

forlorn.description: Pitifully sad and abandoned or lonely.

Hang-Ball.description: A bull who, due to excess male vigor, leaves his herd and lives wildly in the forest.

Greedy.description: A jackal living in the forest with his wife, who becomes obsessed with the idea of obtaining the bull's testicles.

Penny-Hide.description: Two merchant sons in Growing City who represent the extremes of miserliness and generosity toward guests.

Spot.description: A deer who joins the group of friends after fleeing from hunters and becomes a central character in the story.

Himalayan.description: Refers to the Himalayan mountains, symbolizing great strength or hardness.

Lord of All.description: A reference to the supreme deity or God, invoked as the granter of fate and fortune.

king-swans.description: A reference to the regal swans, often symbolic in Indian literature.

emerald-tipped.description: Describes grass with tips as green as emeralds; poetic imagery.

fool’s errand.description: An idiom meaning a pointless or hopeless task.

plover.description: A type of wading bird, referenced in a proverb.

mouse-flesh.description: Meat of a mouse, indicating the jackal's usual food.

cholera.description: An infectious disease, here indicating Penny-Hide's illness.

courtyard.description: An open space surrounded by buildings, common in Indian homes.

penance.description: A religious or spiritual act of self-discipline or repentance.

asylum.description: A place of safety or refuge.

league.description: An old measure of distance, roughly three miles.

grooms.description: Servants who take care of horses, common in royal or wealthy households.

self-prostration.description: The act of humbling oneself completely, often in a physical or spiritual sense.

nectar-draught.description: A poetic phrase for a drink of nectar, symbolizing supreme satisfaction.

suppliant.description: A person making a humble plea to someone in power or authority.

fructify.description: To bear fruit or produce results.

elephant-king.description: The leader of an elephant herd and his retinue who interact with the mice, moving from a position of threat to one of friendship and rescue.

acacia-wood.description: Wood from the acacia tree, native to India and commonly referenced in Indian literature.

fettered.description: Bound or chained, typically referring to being restrained.

dunderheads.description: Foolish or stupid people; an archaic English insult.

willy-nilly.description: Whether one likes it or not; without choice, or in a disorganized manner.

trap.description: A device or enclosure used for capturing animals, here specifically for elephants and Spot.

guy-ropes.description: Ropes used to secure or stabilize something, such as a trap or tent.

prince.description: A royal figure and ruler who commands elephant-trappers and later receives Spot the deer as a pet, becoming astonished by the animal's speech.

holy man.description: A compassionate figure who understands Spot's plight and persuades the prince to release him.

Jump-Up.description: One of the two gaits of deer mentioned in the story, used to avoid snares.

Straightaway.description: The other gait of deer, which Spot knows but is less useful for avoiding traps.

gambol.description: To skip or jump about playfully.

cudgels.description: Short, thick sticks used as weapons.

sorcerers.description: People who claim to have magical powers; magicians.

conjurer.description: A person who performs magic tricks or illusions.

fortress.description: A stronghold or place of defense, here used metaphorically for a place of safety.

prodigy.description: An extraordinary or marvelous event; here, the prince refers to the talking deer as a prodigy.

predestined.description: Determined in advance by fate or destiny.

ointment.description: A smooth substance applied to the skin for healing or soothing.

salves.description: Healing ointments used to soothe the skin.

brace.description: To prepare oneself for something difficult or unpleasant.

brittleness.description: Fragility or tendency to break easily, used metaphorically for the world.
